Hood Heroes – épisode 4 : Momo , le ment: Hood Heroes – Episode 4: Momo, the Mentor of Saint-Michel
La Converse est partie à sa rencontre po: La Converse went to meet him to find out who Mohamed Noredine Mimoun is – before he is “Momo.”
Qui pourrait prétendre vivre dans le qua: Who could claim to live in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood and never have heard of Mohamed Noredine Mimoun, a.k.a. “Momo”? Coordinator of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel and a community worker at Maisonneuve CEGEP, Mohamed Mimoun is the very definition of dedication, especially toward young people, to whom he attaches great importance and in whom he places great hope. This 46-year-old Algerian community worker is already known in political and media circles for his work and for his public statements and positions. But who is he really, this man whom the youth of Saint-Michel consider a “mentor”? La Converse went to meet him to find out who Mohamed Noredine Mimoun is – before he is “Momo.”
« Je suis né en Algérie. Je suis arrivé: “I was born in Algeria. I arrived in France, in Paris, in my twenties as an international student. I was juggling two, even three jobs at once when I arrived, and then I started working in my preferred field,” says Mohamed. His professional experience in Paris didn’t start out as planned, and he decided to open a bookstore: “My wife could see that I wasn’t happy with what I was doing.” His adventure as a bookseller lasted three years, until another reason pushed Mohamed Mimoun to leave Paris, and the European continent, for good.
« Au moment où je suis parti étudier en: “When I left to study in France, I mostly wanted a better life than in Algeria, but I hadn’t done enough research,” Momo says with regret. “It was the late 1990s, and racism was very present; it was something new to me. Seeing that I scared some people simply because of my first name or my appearance was very hard to accept at first. Given who I am and my values, it’s hard to accept that someone doesn’t like me simply because, on the surface, I represent what frightens them. I didn’t want my future children to know that feeling,” he explains.
Pour Mohamed, continuer à vivre en Franc: For Mohamed, continuing to live in France was impossible, but going back to Algeria, his native country, was just as impossible. “Some of my customers at the bookstore were disappointed that I was leaving, but unfortunately the reality remains the same. I loved my neighbourhood, but when I left my little corner, all the prejudices came out, as for every ‘Mohamed,’ and I couldn’t accept that,” he says with regret. So he and his wife headed into the unknown and landed in Canada, in Montréal. Mohamed was already in his thirties.
« Tu ne changes pas un dollar pour 85 so: “You don’t trade a dollar for 85 cents, so I didn’t want to end up in the same situation as in Paris. I wanted to settle down and have a rewarding job connected to what I like to do,” says Mohamed, adding that over the years he has developed a clear idea of what drives him. His Paris experience was a wake-up call for the community worker: “I really like working with people, and I wanted to put my personal experience to use to help others in an immigration context. I told myself I would pass on to people what I had, or didn’t have, when I arrived in France, for example. Because even when you change countries, the situation and the reality stay the same.”
Mohamed veut prendre sa « revanche » sur: Mohamed wants to take his “revenge” on life and on his struggle to survive in France. “I had a lot of problems when I was in France. I had a lot of needs and very little help. I said to myself, ‘Can we get revenge on life and do the opposite, by reaching out to people who have just arrived, or who were born here, who grew up here and who need support and help?’” he wondered, before his wife told him about an opening for a community worker position at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel (FJSM). He got the job, and it felt like a natural fit for the man who would also become a community worker at Maisonneuve CEGEP. Between the FJSM and the college, Momo finds professional and personal fulfilment working with Montréal youth: “I try to plant a seed in these young people who, one day, may be able to change the world. At my level, I can’t change it, but I can have people who will change it.”

Mohamed Mimoun et les jeunes bénévoles d: Mohamed Mimoun and the young volunteers of the Forum Jeunesse Saint-Michel during the “Samedi Itinérant” Photo: Ramy Berkani
« La jeunesse montréalaise, qu’on le veu: “Montréal’s youth, whether we like it or not, are the future of this city and this country. They are tomorrow’s citizens, who will shape the country in their image,” insists Momo about the young people he believes in. Even though he distinguishes between his two community worker jobs (his work at Maisonneuve is more one-on-one than at the forum and takes a more group-based approach), Momo’s goal remains the same: “What I’m trying to do is bring in new community workers from the new generation. And that will help the community a lot, because we have our own way of doing things. We know our culture, we know the problems our young people can face, and we have that ease of connecting with them. Whether you like it or not, when a young person is in contact with a community worker from the same culture, that’s halfway there,” he says.
Et le rôle de l’intervenant ne s’arrête: And the community worker’s role doesn’t stop there. Aware of how disconnected members of this new generation are from the media and political world, Momo wants to make them aware of what awaits them and encourage them to take their destiny into their own hands. “What I want for young people is the place where power is held – where the decisions that are part of public life, of their lives, are made. It’s good to have a good job and a good career, but you have to be part of the game and know the rules. And as long as you have young people who are integrating into that world and who know the rules, you never know whether some of them might end up on boards of directors. That’s what we need!”
Mohamed Mimoun dénonce aussi les préjugé: Mohamed Mimoun also denounces the media’s prejudices about young people in the neighbourhoods. According to him, the media talk about these young people as victims, as people in precarious situations and in need. “There is no recognition of value in the neighbourhoods, no acknowledgement of what a young person can bring or give to their community. That’s why we have to support them. The last time, for example, the young people were at an event where a priority for the neighbourhood had to be decided. They took part in that decision, much to their surprise,” he says with conviction, highlighting the potential for power among these young people from the neighbourhoods. Being proud of your neighbourhood is one thing, but for Momo, you have to go beyond your own reality and “start changing things around you, while staying open to the world.” You have to, as he puts it, “be in contact with others without shutting yourself in the comfort of your neighbourhood.”
L’authenticité est le maître-mot de Moha: Authenticity is Mohamed Mimoun’s watchword. It is what gives him strength day to day, especially with young people: “Having little Momos who succeed me would make me proud, but above all I’d like people to remember my authenticity. That’s what I try to pass on as much as possible to the younger ones. There is nothing more beautiful or more honourable than succeeding while staying yourself and keeping your authenticity.” It is this character trait that won the trust of all these young people.
Que ce soit à Saint-Michel ou à Maisonne: Whether in Saint-Michel or at Maisonneuve, everyone Momo has taken under his wing is unanimous in how they see him: in their eyes, he is a mentor. In school, work, personal life, sports and even love, the Saint-Michel community worker is the ear that every young person comes to confide in. “‘Momo, I met someone; I don’t know if she’s the right person and if I should marry her…’ Looking back, I wonder whether I should tell him if she’s the right person for him or not. Should I be doing that? The bond of trust I built with this kid is what lets him ask me that question today. It’s a pretty special feeling, honestly,” Momo recalls, looking up at the ceiling with a doubtful air.
Cette confiance qu’il suscite chez les j: As for the trust he inspires in young people, we also wonder how he manages to do it. To answer that question, we go to the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel (FJSM) on a Saturday to meet the association’s young volunteers and community workers, all under the guidance of their coordinator. “Momo is both a father and a best friend,” says Imene, an FJSM volunteer. “I had started the process to get an ADD diagnosis, and Mohamed helped and supported me throughout.”
Nessim, un autre bénévole du forum, est: Nessim, another volunteer at the forum, is grateful for everything his community worker gives him: “He’s really like my second dad, always there when you need him. To help you or just to listen. You know you can always count on him.” “If I’m the person I am today, it’s largely thanks to Momo. He gave me my chance and helps me grow a little more every day. He’s my mentor here, my anchor,” says Azzouz, proudly, a protégé who now works as a community worker alongside Momo. Even those who have known him only a short time talk about him as if he had always been part of their lives. That’s the case for Hugo, the FJSM’s newest volunteer: “Whether it’s with communities, young people or even people living on the street, Momo naturally brings people together, regardless of age. You feel valued by his side, and it gives us a lot of strength and motivation.”
« Je ne me suis jamais défini comme un m: “I never defined myself as a mentor. I’m happy that it’s been taken that way, seeing people succeed and say, ‘Momo was a mentor to me.’ If I contributed in one way or another to their success, then great! My personal satisfaction is in that success. Of course it makes me happy that they see me that way!” Momo confides.
<strong>Les « samedis itinérants » ou le: The “Samedis Itinérants,” or the feeling of a job well done
Le « samedi itinérant » est une initiati: The “samedi itinérant” is an initiative started by the FJSM during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was an idea Momo put into action at the urging of the forum’s young volunteers. “The young people didn’t want to sit around doing nothing during that period, so they wanted to make themselves useful,” explains the coordinator. The process is simple: pick up food from a food bank, cook meals in a community kitchen and distribute them to people experiencing homelessness downtown. “This initiative is a meeting between us, the young people, the volunteers and the people experiencing homelessness, where we learn to cook, manage our time and work as a team,” Momo sums up, before explaining the real goal of the initiative.
« Je peux moi-même, seul, préparer à man: “I could, by myself, prepare food and distribute it to homeless people in Montréal – I’ve already done it many times. With that gesture, I would certainly give them a moment of happiness, with a hot meal, but am I going to change the reality of those who live on the street? No! On the other hand – so that you understand the logic and where I’m going with this –, involving young people to do it is essential. Sending them to choose the food, having them cook, going out to meet people experiencing homelessness, that’s where they open their eyes to other realities and become aware. These young people may one day become tomorrow’s decision-makers. They will have that sensitivity to the realities homeless people live, they will learn sharing and making an effort for others. Thanks to this initiative, you multiply the number of young people who get involved and become aware of this reality – it’s no longer just me, Momo, preparing hot meals and handing them out to people in need.”
Joyeux, gentil, rassembleur, généreux ou: Cheerful, kind, unifying, generous, even exceptional: the adjectives young people use to describe Momo keep coming. Whether in his work at the forum or at the CEGEP, Mohamed Noredine Mimoun inspires and motivates everyone he supports and who surrounds him. So who better than one of the first young people to have known him at the forum, Aniss Rizzoug, a.k.a. “Nissou,” to conclude a report on the mentor of Saint-Michel: “Momo never gives up and he’s everywhere – at work, volunteering, with the young people –, he represents us publicly. His only motivation is the success of each one of us, and I have so much respect for that! And thank you for not just being there, but always being there!”
